extractor.note: Partial pass over § 10, § 26, the Appendices section and Section 4, where the reduction is operative rather than thematic.

coverage_note: Covers § 10 (perception and perceptual sense), § 26 (the delimitation of themes for a phenomenological doctrine of association), Section 2 (Appendices) and Section 4 (on static and genetic phenomenological method). The remainder of the volume is not covered.

units.claim: Under the reduction every act has its meant object containing all modalities of being, from which a schism between intentional content and intentional modal-character arises.
units.quote: When we carry out the phenomenological reduction, every "act" has its meant object containing all modalities of being.

units.claim: Within the reduction what is there is not the world as reality with its causalities but only phenomena in their intentionality, which excludes an objective psychophysical account of association.
units.quote: Within the phenomenological reduction, what is there is not the world as reality with its causalities, but only phenomena in their intentionality.

units.claim: Appendix 8 distinguishes two types of transcendental reduction with respect to remembering, in the course of treating the apodicticity of memory.
units.quote: two types of transcendental reduction with respect to remembering

units.claim: It is asked whether phenomenological truths gained through the egological reduction can claim intersubjective validity, since truths adopted by the phenomenological ego do not straightforwardly have that sense.
units.quote: Husserl addresses the question whether phenomenological truths, gained through the egological reduction, can claim intersubjective validity.

units.claim: After the phenomenological reduction the ego can say ego cogito, ego sum in absolute Cartesian evidence.
units.quote: After the phenomenological reduction, the ego can say *ego cogito, ego sum* in absolute Cartesian evidence.
